concept: A usable estimate of almost any quantity comes from decomposing it into independently guessable factors, multiplying them while tracking units, and aiming for the right order of magnitude rather than a precise figure.
across: Space & Astronomy — Frank Drake's 1961 equation for the number of communicating galactic civilizations is the same Fermi-chain method, and also shows where it breaks: several of its factors are uncertain by many orders of magnitude, not just a factor of a few.
claim: A disciplined chain of rough, independently-guessable factors can land within a factor of two of ground truth even with no instruments at all (Fermi at Trinity, 10,000 tons guessed vs. a measured yield of 18.6-24.8 kt) — but the same method, applied to the Drake equation, shows that when individual factors are uncertain by many orders of magnitude rather than a factor of a few, the chain stops producing a trustworthy number at all. Decomposition is not by itself a guarantee of accuracy; it only works as well as its least-certain link.
label: settled
evidence: Fermi's 1945 Trinity memo; J. I. Katz, "Fermi at Trinity" (Nuclear Technology, 2021); H. D. Selby et al., 2021 Trinity yield reassessment; Drake equation history checked via web search (Green Bank, Nov. 1961).

concept: Constant-percentage growth compounds, and a logarithmic scale turns that compounding into a straight line whose slope is the growth rate.
across: AI — OpenAI's 2018 'AI and Compute' analysis found training compute for the largest AI runs grew ~300,000-fold from 2012-2018, doubling roughly every 3.4 months, read with the same straight-line-on-a-log-plot method Moore used on transistor counts.
claim: A trend line fitted to past compounding data describes the rate that held in the past, not a law bound to continue — Moore's own 1975 revision of his 1965 forecast is the method's inventor making that correction in public, and it is a recurring failure mode whenever people extrapolate a 'law' from a short run of real data.
label: settled
evidence: Gordon Moore, 'Cramming more components onto integrated circuits' (Electronics, 1965) and his 1975 IEEE paper revising the doubling period, both checked via web search against the Computer History Museum's and IEEE's own accounts this run.

concept: Scale an object up with its shape fixed and area grows as the square of its size while volume and weight grow as the cube, so any property depending on their ratio changes with size.
across: Engineering — Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638) used the same square-cube argument to show a scaled-up wooden beam collapses under its own weight, which is why structural design is never just a bigger photograph of a smaller design.
claim: The square-cube law is settled geometry, but Kleiber's widely used 3/4-power rule for metabolic rate is not: West, Brown and Enquist's 1997 theoretical derivation from branching supply networks and White and Seymour's 2003 empirical re-analysis of 619 mammal species (finding closer to 2/3) still disagree, nearly a century after Kleiber's original 1932 study, on both the exact exponent and why it holds — a reminder that a number everyone uses is not automatically a number everyone has agreed on.
label: debated
evidence: J. B. S. Haldane, "On Being the Right Size" (Harper's Magazine, 1926); Max Kleiber (1932); West, Brown & Enquist, Science 276 (1997); White & Seymour, PNAS (2003); Galileo, Two New Sciences (1638). All checked via web search this run.

concept: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a quantity, and the second derivative tells you whether that rate is itself speeding up or slowing down.
across: Engineering — Nicolas Minorsky's 1922 PID (proportional-integral-derivative) controller, whose derivative term damps overshoot by reacting to how fast an error is changing.
claim: The Keeling CO2 record shows two separately measurable facts that look contradictory but are not: the instantaneous rate is negative every Northern Hemisphere summer, while the year-over-year trend rate has been positive every year since 1958 and has itself climbed from under 1 ppm/yr in the 1960s to over 2 ppm/yr in the 2010s (a positive second derivative).
label: settled
evidence: Scripps Institution of Oceanography Keeling Curve program history; NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory Mauna Loa CO2 growth-rate figures. Checked via web search this run.

concept: An integral adds a rate times a thin slice of time, across every slice, to build an exact total, and the fundamental theorem of calculus says accumulating a rate and differentiating the result undo each other.
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — the FDA's bioequivalence standard compares the area under a drug's blood-concentration-versus-time curve (AUC) between a generic and the brand original, requiring the 90% confidence interval of their ratio to fall within 80-125%.
claim: The Deepwater Horizon spill's contested totals (BP's ~2.45 million barrels vs. the government's ~4.9 million vs. Judge Barbier's court finding of 3.19 million discharged) show that uncertainty in an integrated total almost always traces back to uncertainty in the underlying rate, not to the arithmetic of integration itself — a distinction worth separating in any debate over a disputed cumulative number.
label: debated
evidence: U.S. Department of the Interior's 2 Aug 2010 Flow Rate Technical Group release; AP/Jurist/Marine Technology News reporting on Judge Carl Barbier's January 2015 ruling. Checked via web search this run.

concept: A differential equation (dN/dt = -kN) states a quantity's rate of change in terms of its own current value; with a known starting value it fixes the quantity's entire future and past, giving radioactive decay a fixed half-life and, run backwards, a clock.
across: History — Colin Renfrew's Before Civilization (1973): calibrated radiocarbon dates made Malta's temples older than Egypt's pyramids and Stonehenge older than Mycenae, overturning Near-East diffusion as the explanation for European prehistory.
claim: Only one of radiocarbon dating's two assumptions needed empirical testing: the decay rate k is settled nuclear physics and needed no check, but the starting atmospheric carbon-14 level was an empirical guess that Libby's 1949 Curve of Knowns tested against independently known ages, and that later calibration curves (Suess 1967, today's IntCal) have had to keep correcting.
label: settled
evidence: Arnold & Libby, Science 110 (1949): 678-680; ACS National Historic Chemical Landmark materials; 1962 Cambridge Radiocarbon Conference half-life revision; checked via web search this run.

concept: Growth limited by a ceiling traces an S-shaped (logistic) curve, dN/dt = rN(1-N/K), whose growth rate peaks at the inflection point N=K/2; before that point the data cannot identify the ceiling K, because very different ceilings fit the same early numbers almost equally well.
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — Kermack and McKendrick's 1927 epidemic model, whose final-size relation sets an outbreak's S-shaped ceiling from transmissibility and immunity rather than from population size as a free parameter.
claim: Pearl and Reed's 1920 logistic fit to 120 years of US census data (1790-1910) was an excellent fit to shape and wrong by over 130 million people on the ceiling (197 million predicted vs. 331 million counted in 2020), because American growth in 1920 sat just before its own fitted inflection point (~1914), where the data could not yet distinguish that ceiling from many others — the general trap of fitting a bounded-growth model before it has visibly bent.
label: settled
evidence: R. Pearl and L. J. Reed, PNAS 6 (June 1920): 275-288; US Census Bureau's Nov. 20, 1967 200-million milestone and 2020 Census count; both checked via web search this run.

concept: Optimization: at a smooth interior optimum the derivative is zero, so the loss from missing grows with the square of the miss (flat optimum); constraints and the choice of objective move the best point
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — Murray's law (1926): minimizing pumping power plus blood-volume upkeep gives flow proportional to radius cubed, so at a vessel branch the parent's radius cubed equals the sum of the daughters'
claim: Setting the derivative of a two-term cost to zero gives the honeybee cell's cap angle (arccos(-1/3) = 109°28'16"), and a 2-minute-of-arc miss would waste under one part in a million of the wax, so Koenig's 'two-minute error' was his own arithmetic mistake (Maclaurin, 1743), not the bees'. The mathematics is settled; what counts as 'optimal' depends on the objective chosen, which is where values enter.
label: settled
evidence: Cap angle, wax-area formula and the 2-minute loss checked numerically against an explicit 3-D model of the cell (loss about 1.2e-6 s^2, under 6e-7 of the wax); Maraldi 1712 / Koenig c.1739 (109°26') / Maclaurin 1743 / Fejes Toth 1964 (under 0.35% of the opening's area) via web search; ORNL/DOE speed-fuel averages and TRB Special Report 204 (167,000 bbl/day, under 2% of highway fuel) via web search.

concept: Quantities with size and direction are vectors; the relative velocity of two movers (v_B minus v_A) decides whether and when they meet, and for craft holding course and speed a collision course is exactly a steady bearing with shrinking range.
across: Space & Astronomy — Gemini 4 (June 1965): James McDivitt could not close on his spent Titan upper stage, because in orbit gravity bends both paths and the straight-line relative-velocity rule stops applying.
claim: COLREGs Rule 7 writes a piece of vector mathematics into law: it deems collision risk to exist if an approaching vessel's compass bearing does not appreciably change, which for two craft holding course and speed is exactly the condition that their relative velocity points straight back along the line of sight. By contrast, the CAB's finding on the 1956 Grand Canyon collision was only that the pilots did not see each other in time, so the same geometry is a mechanism consistent with that finding, not part of it.
label: settled
evidence: Rule 7(d)(i) wording ('the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change') confirmed in several reproductions of the COLREGs via web search; CAB probable-cause wording confirmed via FAA and Aviation Safety Network summaries; the vector condition checked by working the 10-nautical-mile ship example in components and by minimising squared distance (collision at 40 minutes).

concept: A mathematical proof deduces a claim from axioms and earlier results so it holds in every case at once, with a certainty no number of examples can give, but only if every step is valid and only relative to its axioms.
across: Law — In re Winship (1970): due process requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute a crime, a threshold of confidence reached from evidence rather than a deduction from axioms; Justice Harlan's concurrence rests it on a value judgment that convicting an innocent man is far worse than letting a guilty man go free.
claim: Evidence from cases can fail at the first untested case: n^2 + n + 41 is prime for every n from 0 to 39 and fails at n = 40 (1,681 = 41 x 41), and Euler's 1769 sums-of-powers conjecture stood for nearly two centuries until 27^5 + 84^5 + 110^5 + 133^5 = 144^5 (both sides 61,917,364,224) — whereas a proof covers all cases at once, conditional on its axioms and on every step being valid.
label: settled
evidence: The arithmetic (the n^2 + n + 41 run and its failure at n = 40, and the 27/84/110/133/144 fifth-power identity) was checked by direct computation this run. Web search was unavailable, so the attribution of the second counterexample to Lander and Parkin (1966) and the 1769 date rest on standard references not re-checked against a live source.

concept: Probability puts weights on a complete list of outcomes; expected value is their weighted average, the long-run average per try (law of large numbers) and the basis of fair division in Pascal and Fermat's 1654 problem of points, but not by itself a rule for one person's one-time risk.
across: Philosophy — Pascal's Wager in the Pensées (published 1670): expected value with an infinite payoff, challenged by Diderot's 'imam could reason the same way' (many gods) objection, which is an incomplete sample space.
claim: An average gain across a population (about three added years of life expectancy from universal variolation in Daniel Bernoulli's 1760 model) does not by itself settle whether one person should accept an immediate risk of death (d'Alembert's objection), so the choice between the state's standpoint and the individual's is a moral question the arithmetic cannot decide.
label: value
evidence: Checked via web search: Bernoulli's memoir read to the Paris Academy 30 April 1760, printed 1766, life expectancy 26 y 7 m to 29 y 9 m, using Halley's 1693 table; d'Alembert's Academy lecture of 12 November 1760 and Opuscules mathématiques vol. 2 (1761), arguing a modest average gain would not tempt an individual to accept immediate risk of death, with Bernoulli reasoning as a state and d'Alembert as an individual. The 1-in-200 and roughly one-in-ten figures rest on secondary accounts of the memoir, not the memoir itself.

concept: A distribution's tail decides what 'extreme' means: bell-curve tails fall like e^(-k^2/2), so a 6-sigma event is about 1 in a billion, while a power-law tail P(X>x) ~ x^(-alpha) falls only as a power, so the largest event on record is a poor guide to the next. Return periods are annual odds (a '100-year' flood has a 26% chance within 30 years), not schedules.
across: Sociology — Zipf's rank-size rule for city sizes (2020 Census: New York City 8.80 million, Los Angeles 44% of that, Chicago 31%, Houston 26%) and Gabaix's 1999 Gibrat's-law explanation of a power-law city-size tail.
claim: Fukushima Daiichi's documented design numbers (3.1 m from the 1960 Chile tsunami; 5.7 m after the 2002 JSCE method; a 2008 in-house trial calculation of up to 15.7 m; roughly 13-15 m measured in 2011) show that a design basis is a chosen probability, not a physical constant, and Japanese courts have split on whether the 2011 wave was foreseeable (criminal acquittals finalized in 2025; a 2022 civil liability ruling reversed by the Tokyo High Court in June 2025).
label: debated
evidence: TEPCO tsunami-survey releases (April/July 2011, 2012); Japan Atomic Energy Commission briefing; Carnegie Endowment 2012 exchange with TEPCO; press reports of the 2008 calculation and of the 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2025 court rulings; all checked via web search.

concept: A network's structure (degree distribution, clustering, hubs and a few long-range shortcuts) decides how fast things spread across it and how failures cascade through it; the typical path in an unclustered network is ln N / ln k, and a few shortcuts restore short paths to a clustered one.
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — the roundworm C. elegans nervous system (White, Southgate, Thomson & Brenner 1986), which Watts & Strogatz (Nature, 1998) showed is a small-world network: far more clustered than a random network of the same size, with nearly as short paths.
claim: In the Watts-Strogatz small-world model (a ring of 1,000 nodes, each linked to its 10 nearest neighbours), rewiring only about 1% of links as random shortcuts cuts the average path from about 50 steps to about 9 while clustering stays at about 0.65 of the original 0.67, so a handful of long-range ties, not dense connectivity, is what makes a clustered world small. This is mathematics, not a claim that any real network is built this way.
label: settled
evidence: Own simulation of the model (N=1000, k=10, 20 runs per rewiring probability, results: p=0 L=50.5 C=0.667; p=0.01 L=8.8 C=0.646; p=1 L=3.27 C=0.009), consistent with the pattern Watts & Strogatz report in Nature 393:440-442 (1998); that the paper exists and reports high clustering with short paths was confirmed by web search at curriculum-build time, but its figures were not re-opened this run.

concept: Game theory: Nash equilibrium, the prisoner's dilemma and the shadow of the future (TIT FOR TAT)
across: History — the First World War live-and-let-live trench truces (Ashworth 1980; Axelrod 1984, ch. 4)
claim: With Axelrod's payoffs (T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0), reciprocal cooperation between self-interested parties is stable only if the chance of meeting again is at least 2/3 (an expected game of three rounds): cooperation is sustained by a long enough shadow of the future, not by good character, and the same mechanism sustains cooperation whether or not it benefits people outside the game.
label: settled
evidence: Threshold derived algebraically and confirmed numerically by a best-response calculation over all strategies (TIT FOR TAT is a best reply to itself exactly when w >= 2/3); web search confirmed Axelrod's Proposition 2 (TIT FOR TAT is collectively stable if and only if w is large enough) and the 1980 tournament facts (JCR 24(1) and 24(3)). The theorem is settled; how far it explains real-world cooperation is debated (Rapoport, Seale and Colman 2015; Gowa on the trench case).

concept: Bayes' theorem and base rates: posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds
across: Engineering — the Bayesian search for Air France Flight 447 (Metron for the BEA; wreckage found April 2011)
claim: A rare-looking piece of evidence is strong only relative to the rival explanation: Meadow's 1-in-73-million figure for two cot deaths was reached by squaring 1 in 8,543 (assuming independence), the Royal Statistical Society said in October 2001 it had no statistical basis, and even a correct figure would be only the likelihood half of the calculation, with the prior for the rival (double murder) just as small.
label: settled
evidence: Royal Statistical Society statement (Oct 2001) and Jan 2002 letter to the Lord Chancellor; National Archives record of R v Clark [2003] EWCA Crim 1020 (convictions quashed after hearing 28-29 Jan 2003, chiefly on undisclosed microbiology); Wellington law review and OpenLearn accounts of the 8,543 x 8,543 calculation and the independence assumption; all checked via web search.

concept: Sampling and the margin of error: random error is computable and shrinks as 1/sqrt(n); bias from who is in the frame and who answers does not shrink with n
across: Law — Department of Commerce v. U.S. House of Representatives, 525 U.S. 316 (1999): the Court held 5-4 that the Census Act bars statistical sampling for congressional apportionment, after the Census Bureau planned random-sample follow-up of non-responding households and a ~750,000-housing-unit coverage survey to correct undercounts
claim: A survey's margin of error covers only random sampling error, which falls with the square root of sample size; the dominant risk in modern public statistics is non-response bias, which sample size cannot fix. BLS's Current Population Survey household response rate fell from 86.4% (Feb 2016) to 65.9% (Feb 2026), and its own monthly-change interval for the unemployment rate is about ±0.3 points at 90% confidence (stated for a rate near 6%), so a 0.1-point move (4.1% to 4.2%, Aug to Sep 2026) is within noise.
label: settled
evidence: BLS Employment Situation technical note and Table A-1 (September 2026 data, read directly on bls.gov); BLS household-survey response-rate table (Feb 2016 to Feb 2026); the Supreme Court's published opinion in 525 U.S. 316, read in the U.S. Reports bound volume on supremecourt.gov; sampling arithmetic recomputed (n=1,000 gives ±3.1 points; n=2.4 million gives ±0.06).

concept: A p-value or sigma level is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null model were true, computed inside an error model; it cannot see a systematic error that model leaves out, and it says nothing about how plausible the claim was beforehand.
across: Space & Astronomy — BICEP2 (March 2014) rejected 'no primordial signal' at 7 sigma, but a 2015 joint analysis with Planck found strong evidence for galactic dust and no statistically significant evidence for the primordial signal: a significance quoted against a model that underestimated a real source of signal.
claim: OPERA's 'six sigma' faster-than-light result already included its estimated systematic uncertainty (60.7 ns / sqrt(6.9^2 + 7.4^2) = 6.0), so the failure was not neglect of systematic error but an unlisted one: a fiber-optic timing-link fault of about 73 ns, roughly ten times the 7.4 ns allowance. A significance level is only as sound as the error model it is computed inside, and more data would have raised the false significance (to about 8 sigma at 100x the events), not lowered it.
label: settled
evidence: OPERA Collaboration, arXiv:1109.4897 (60.7 ± 6.9 stat ± 7.4 sys ns, overall significance 6.0 sigma); a secondary paper confirming that adding stat and sys in quadrature gives 6 sigma; OPERA's later paper reporting a fibre delay 73.2 ns larger than its 2006-07 calibration; CERN statements of 23 Sep 2011 and 8 Jun 2012; Lyons, 'Open statistical issues in particle physics' (2008). Checked via web search this run; the quadrature arithmetic and the 10x/100x-events figures were recomputed here.

concept: Correlation, confounding and Simpson's paradox: a combined rate is a weighted average of subgroup rates, so unequal weights can reverse a comparison
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — Charig et al. (BMJ 1986) kidney-stone treatments, analysed as Simpson's paradox by Julious & Mullee (BMJ 1994)
claim: In Berkeley's 1973 data for its six largest departments, the pooled 14-point admission gap (44.5% of men, 30.4% of women) is almost entirely a difference in which departments men and women applied to (mix effect -14.3 points; within-department rate effect +0.1 at the women's mix), and women's rate was higher in four of the six departments.
label: settled
evidence: Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, Science 187 (1975), confirmed via web search for the university-wide counts (8,442 men / 3,738 admitted; 4,321 women / 1,494 admitted) and the finding of a small bias in women's favor once pooled by department; the six-department counts match the totals in the standard published data set (2,691 men / 1,198 admitted; 1,835 women / 557 admitted), and the decomposition was computed from those counts. The interpretation of why women applied where they did is a separate, open question that the lesson labels as debated.

concept: Whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated, cases extreme on one are on average less extreme on the other (regression to the mean); the regression line has slope r in standard units, so a fraction 1 - r of an extreme is expected to fade, and the population's spread is preserved because r^2 + (1 - r^2) = 1.
across: Psychology — Daniel Kahneman's Israeli Air Force flight instructors (Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011, ch. 17), who misread regression to the mean in cadets' maneuvers as the effect of praise and punishment.
claim: Selecting cases because one measurement was extreme guarantees apparent improvement on re-measurement whenever the two measurements are imperfectly correlated, so any before-and-after evaluation of an intervention aimed at the worst cases (speed cameras sited after crash clusters, turnaround grants for lowest-scoring schools, regulation after a scandal) needs a comparison group chosen by the same rule.
label: settled
evidence: Derived from the least-squares line (slope r in standard units) and checked numerically by simulation this run: 1.5 million bivariate-normal pairs at r = 0.5 gave a mean second measurement of about 1.01 SD for cases at 2 SD, a variance split of 0.25 + 0.75, about 12.4% of such cases landing at least as high as 2, and about 82% of cases at 2 SD or more having started less extreme; a Gamma-Poisson count model (mean 4, r = 0.5) reproduced the stylized 10 -> 7 expectation. Historical sources (Galton 1886, Kahneman 2011) were not re-checked because web search was unavailable.

concept: Randomized controlled trials: random assignment sets selection bias to zero on average, so a difference in outcomes estimates the causal effect plus chance
across: Computing — Bing's 2012 ad-headline A/B test, a randomized experiment that raised revenue about 12% (Kohavi & Thomke, Harvard Business Review, 2017)
claim: Observational studies of hormone therapy (Nurses' Health Study, RR 0.56 for major coronary disease; a 1991 pooled review, RR 0.56) pointed to about 44% less heart disease, but the randomized Women's Health Initiative trial of combined estrogen plus progestin found no protection (coronary hazard ratio 1.29, nominal 95% CI 1.02-1.63, widening to 0.85-1.97 when adjusted for sequential monitoring), which ruled out protection of the size claimed without by itself proving harm. The comparison is not perfectly like for like: the 1991 paper concerned estrogen therapy and the trial tested estrogen with a progestin, and how much of the gap is healthy-user bias versus other design differences is debated.
label: settled
evidence: WHI principal results, JAMA 288:321-333 (2002) and the labelling tables reproducing its coronary hazard ratio; Stampfer et al., NEJM 325:756-762 (1991) and Stampfer & Colditz, Prev Med 20:47-63 (1991); Rossouw et al., JAMA 297:1465-1477 (2007), all checked via web search this run. Settled for the enrolled population (mean age about 63); the explanation of the gap is debated.

concept: When an accident of nature, history or policy sorts people into treated and untreated groups as if at random, comparing how the groups change (difference-in-differences) can reveal a cause no one could randomize, but only if the groups would have moved in parallel without the treatment.
across: Biology, Medicine & Health — the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944-45 as a natural experiment in prenatal development (Ravelli, Stein & Susser, NEJM 1976; Heijmans et al., PNAS 2008)
claim: Whether higher speed limits cost lives can only be answered by natural experiments, and their estimates differ in size and even direction: Friedman, Hedeker and Richter (2009) attribute an estimated 12,545 deaths (3.2% of road deaths, 1995-2005; 95% CI about 8,700 to 16,400) to the 1995 repeal of the national limit, while Lave and Elias (1994) found the 1987 rise to 65 mph lowered statewide fatality rates by 3.4% to 5.1% (different periods and roads; a critic disputed their method). Whether faster travel is worth an estimated loss of life is a separate value question the estimates cannot settle.
label: debated
evidence: Checked via web search this run: Friedman, Hedeker & Richter, Am J Public Health 99(9):1626-1631 (2009), abstract figures (12,545 deaths, CI 8,739-16,352, 3.2%, 9.1% rural interstates); Lave & Elias, Accident Analysis & Prevention 26(1):49-62 (1994), 3.4%-5.1% reduction and mechanisms, with Griffith's 1995 discussion; National Highway System Designation Act signed 28 Nov 1995 (FHWA/Federal Register).

concept: Replication and publication bias: significance filtering, low power and flexible analysis inflate published effects
across: Psychology — Open Science Collaboration (Science, 2015) repeated 100 studies: 97% of originals significant, about 36% of replications, effects about half the original size
claim: When only significant results from low-powered studies reach print, the published average overstates the true effect even if nobody cheats: in the worked case (true effect 0.2 SD, standard error 0.2) only about 17% of studies cross p<0.05 and those average about 0.5, roughly 2.5 times the truth, so an exact repeat falls about 60%.
label: settled
evidence: The arithmetic was recomputed from the normal distribution (threshold 1.96 x SE = 0.39; power about 0.17; mean of significant estimates about 0.50; PPV 20/70 = 0.29 for R = 1:10, power 0.2, alpha 0.05). The real-world magnitudes (Amgen 6 of 53, OSC 97% to 36%, Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology effects about 85% smaller) come from the curriculum's research notes and could not be re-checked by web search.

concept: Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, people optimize the number rather than the goal it indicated, so the measure drifts from reality and can move against it; the toy model M = G + gap shows effort flowing to whichever lever (goal or gap) is cheaper.
across: AI — specification gaming (Krakovna et al., DeepMind blog, April 2020): in an example from Popov et al. (2017), a simulated robot arm rewarded for the height of a red Lego block's bottom face flipped the block instead of stacking it.
claim: A policy target can be gamed and still work: England's NHS targets showed gaming (Bevan and Hood 2006 report a spike in ambulance response times at the 8-minute line), yet Propper et al. (2010), comparing England with Scotland, found the targets still shortened long hospital waits with no evident diversion of activity or drop in patient health at discharge. Evidence that a measure is gamed is therefore not evidence that it failed, and the net effect of targets is argued.
label: debated
evidence: Bevan and Hood, Public Administration 84(3):517-538 (2006), ambulance response-time distributions; Propper, Sutton, Whitnall and Windmeijer, Journal of Public Economics 94(3-4):318-335 (2010), England-Scotland natural experiment (abstract-level findings). Both checked via web search; full texts not opened.

concept: The car's rise can be read in four kinds of numbers (energy density, a steadily falling price, S-curve adoption, and harms as rates with confounders in view), but the chain of need, invention, constraint, engineering, financing, regulation, adoption, consequences and feedback runs as a loop rather than a line.
across: Energy, Chemistry & Materials — Bertha Benz's ligroin: burning a hydrocarbon releases bond energy (Day 70, Combustion and energy density)
claim: US automobile registrations grew about 2,900-fold between 1900 and 1929, from about 8,000 to about 23 million, which is roughly 32 percent a year compounded and a doubling about every 2.5 years, while Bertha Benz's 1888 fuel purchase at a pharmacy shows how little supporting infrastructure existed at the start.
label: settled
evidence: Federal Highway Administration, Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200, read via web search: 8,000 automobiles in 1900 and 23,060,421 privately owned automobiles in 1929 (23,120,897 with publicly owned). The growth rate is my arithmetic from the two endpoints. The pharmacy purchase and the later 'first filling station' label were checked via Britannica and other accounts.
